Hoised
hoizd
v. (hoisted, raised up; rendering Greek epairo)
Past tense of hoise, the older form of hoist — a seaman's word for raising sail. It survives in Shakespeare's “hoist with his own petard” and in one verse of Acts.

Biblical Definition

Hoised means hoisted. In the wreck narrative of Acts 27 the sailors, having cut the anchors, “hoised up the mainsail to the wind, and made toward shore” (Act 27:40). The word marks the moment of committed action in one of Scripture's great providence stories: every human skill is spent — anchors, rudder bands, sail — and every life is saved exactly as God had told Paul beforehand.

Webster 1828 Definition

Webster (1828) gives hoise as to lift or raise, especially aboard ship — noting hoist as the form that displaced it.

expand to see more

HOISE, v.t. To lift; to raise; to heave; particularly, to raise by means of tackle, as a sail. [Now written hoist.] Acts 27.

Key Scripture

Act 27:40 — "And when they had taken up the anchors, they committed themselves unto the sea, and loosed the rudder bands, and hoised up the mainsail to the wind, and made toward shore."

Act 27:22 — "And now I exhort you to be of good cheer: for there shall be no loss of any man's life among you, but of the ship."

Act 27:31 — "Paul said to the centurion and to the soldiers, Except these abide in the ship, ye cannot be saved."

Psa 107:23 — "They that go down to the sea in ships, that do business in great waters;"

Modern Corruption

Modern versions say hoisted; nothing is lost in the word, but the chapter's doctrine — absolute promise working through ordinary seamanship — is regularly split into either fatalism or self-help.

expand to see more

Acts 27 holds together what the church keeps pulling apart. God promises categorically that no life shall be lost (Act 27:22–24); Paul then insists with equal force that “except these abide in the ship, ye cannot be saved” (Act 27:31). The promise does not make the sailors idle, and the seamanship does not make the promise conditional. The hoised mainsail is means inside decree.

Fatalism cuts the sail loose — if God has promised, why labour? Self-reliance cuts the promise loose — it was good sailing that beached the ship. Luke's narrative refuses both: they hoised the sail because God had promised, and all came safe to land because they hoised the sail. That is how providence ordinarily works, at sea and in salvation history.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Greek epairo (G1869), to lift up — the word used of hoisting the sail, of lifting up eyes and voices, and of the Lord's ascension.

expand to see more

Greek epairo (G1869) — to lift, raise; the mainsail of Acts 27:40, the lifted eyes of Luke 18:13, and the Lord taken up in Acts 1:9.

Usage

"“They… hoised up the mainsail to the wind, and made toward shore” — means inside decree."

"“There shall be no loss of any man's life among you” — the promise the sail served."

"“Except these abide in the ship, ye cannot be saved” — the necessity the promise employed."
